prompt: A count of one day of November on `events_by_month` showed one scan, on `events_2025_11`. What did the planner do?
hint: It compared two things it had.

choices.text: Read the other months and found nothing
choices.why: They were not in the plan at all, so they were never opened.

choices.text: Compared bounds and kept November
choices.why: Right: that is plan-time pruning, from the values written in the query.

choices.text: Used an index on `at`
choices.why: There is no index on at; inside November it was a sequential scan.

choices.text: Asked the statistics which month is busiest
choices.why: Statistics estimate rows; pruning uses the bounds.

prompt: Counting one day took 216.7 ms on `events` and how many milliseconds on `events_by_month`?
hint: The second EXPLAIN ANALYZE in the section.

prompt: `WHERE at >= '2025-12-20'` kept two partitions. Which ones, and why two?
hint: Which intervals can hold an instant after the 20th of December?

choices.text: November and December, the two nearest
choices.why: November ends before the 20th of December, so nothing in it can match.

choices.text: December and January
choices.why: Right: both intervals overlap 'from the 20th of December on'.

choices.text: December only, plus a copy of the plan
choices.why: January's interval also overlaps the condition, empty or not.

choices.text: October and December, the ones with most rows
choices.why: Row counts play no part; only the bounds do.

prompt: A dashboard always asks for the last 90 days, and the table holds exactly 90 days partitioned by month. What will pruning save it?
hint: It pays in proportion to what it skips.

choices.text: About two thirds, as for the one-day query
choices.why: The day query skipped two months; this one needs all of them.

choices.text: All of the reading, because pruning replaces the scan
choices.why: Pruning chooses partitions; the surviving ones are still read.

choices.text: Almost nothing
choices.why: Right: every partition overlaps the 90 days, and it still pays the overhead lesson 17 measured.

choices.text: Half, because the planner prunes every other month
choices.why: The planner keeps every partition whose interval overlaps; there is no alternating.

prompt: What does `Subplans Removed: 3` under an `Append` tell you?
hint: It never appears with plan-time pruning.

choices.text: Three partitions were dropped when execution started
choices.why: Right: the plan was built for all four and pruned at run time.

choices.text: Three partitions were deleted from the table
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; they were left out of this execution.

choices.text: The planner removed three useless joins
choices.why: There is no join here; the subplans are partition scans.

choices.text: Three workers did not start
choices.why: Workers Launched said 2, as planned.

prompt: Why does a prepared statement under a generic plan need run-time pruning?
hint: What does the planner see instead of a date?

choices.text: Prepared statements disable pruning at planning to save memory
choices.why: Nothing is disabled; there is simply no value to compare yet.

choices.text: The planner sees `$1`, not a date
choices.why: Right: the plan must work for any value, so the bounds are compared when $1 arrives.

choices.text: Generic plans are always slower and need help
choices.why: The pruned generic plan read one month, the same work as the custom one.

choices.text: The driver sends the date after the query has finished
choices.why: The value arrives with EXECUTE, before execution starts.

prompt: In the subquery plan, October and November say `(never executed)` and January shows an actual time. Why the difference?
hint: Compare each interval with the last order's day.

choices.text: January is empty, so it is always executed
choices.why: Being empty does not decide it; its interval does.

choices.text: October and November were pruned at planning
choices.why: They are in the plan; plan-time pruning would have left them out entirely.

choices.text: January's interval could still hold rows after the cut-off
choices.why: Right: only partitions entirely before $1 were skipped.

choices.text: The workers ran out before reaching October
choices.why: Skipped partitions are a decision about bounds, not about workers.

prompt: Setting `plan_cache_mode = ___` makes a prepared statement use one plan for every value from its first execution.
hint: The value the lesson used.

prompt: Why did `WHERE date(at) = '2025-11-10'` read all four partitions?
hint: What are the bounds made of?

choices.text: Because `date()` is slow
choices.why: Its speed is not the issue; it hides the range from the planner.

choices.text: It is not a range of `at`
choices.why: Right: the bounds are values of at, and a function of at is not at.

choices.text: Because November's partition was locked
choices.why: Nothing held a lock; the plan simply contained all four.

choices.text: Because the statistics on `at` were stale
choices.why: Statistics do not decide which partitions are in the plan.

prompt: Which rewrite of `WHERE at::date = '2025-11-10'` lets the planner prune?
hint: Put the column alone on one side.

choices.why: Still a function of at; it read all four partitions.
Right: a range on the column itself, which section 02 pruned to November.

choices.text: `WHERE extract(day FROM at) = 10`
choices.why: A function of at again, and it matches the 10th of every month.

choices.text: `WHERE to_char(at, 'YYYY-MM-DD') = '2025-11-10'`
choices.why: A string made from at is no more prunable than date(at).

prompt: Customer 42's events on `events_by_month` gave an `Append` with an index scan per month. What would the same query give on a table with twelve monthly partitions?
hint: Does the condition say which month?

choices.text: One scan, because the planner learns which month holds the customer
choices.why: The planner learns nothing from earlier runs; customer_id says nothing about months.

choices.text: Twelve probes
choices.why: Right: a condition on another column visits every partition.

choices.text: An error, as the key is missing from the query
choices.why: Queries without the key run fine; they just cannot prune.

choices.text: Four, because only four months have rows
choices.why: Empty partitions are still in the plan; January was scanned though empty.

prompt: Which of these conditions on `events_by_month` can be pruned? Choose all that apply.
hint: The key, alone, against values.

choices.why: Right: it kept December and January.

choices.text: `at >= $1 AND at < $1 + interval '1 day'` in a prepared statement
choices.why: Right: at run time, with Subplans Removed.

choices.text: `at >= (SELECT max(placed_at) FROM orders) - interval '1 day'`
choices.why: Right: during execution, the skipped months marked never executed.

choices.text: `extract(month FROM at) = 11`
choices.why: A function of at; all four partitions were read.

choices.text: `customer_id = 42`
choices.why: Not the key; every partition was probed.

prompt: Planning customer 42's query took about 1 ms on `events_by_month`. How long on `events_by_day`?
hint: Planning Time in the grep.

choices.text: About the same, since the data is the same
choices.why: The time goes into the plan, which has 365 children instead of four.

choices.text: About 30 ms
choices.why: Right: 30.3 and 32.5 ms, around thirty times as long.

choices.text: Under 1 ms, because the partitions are smaller
choices.why: Smaller partitions do not make planning cheaper; more of them make it dearer.

choices.text: Several seconds
choices.why: It was tens of milliseconds, not seconds.

prompt: The one-day query on `events_by_day` read one partition, yet planning took 3.2 ms against 0.6 on the monthly table. Why?
hint: Pruning itself is work.

choices.text: The day partition had no statistics
choices.why: The file ran VACUUM ANALYZE on every partition.

choices.text: It pruned at run time instead
choices.why: The plan named one partition; it was pruned at planning.

choices.text: Pruning still looks at every partition's bounds
choices.why: Right: finding the survivors means looking at 365 sets of bounds.

choices.text: Daily partitions are planned in a loop by the DO block
choices.why: The DO block only created the tables; it plays no part in planning.

prompt: A query that spends 30 ms planning runs 1,000 times a second. How many processor-seconds a second does planning alone need?
hint: Milliseconds times runs, in seconds.

prompt: Order the three questions the lesson asks before choosing a partition count.
hint: Start with why the table is partitioned at all.
items: What is the slice that ages?
What do the queries that cannot prune cost?
What do the queries that can prune gain?
trap: The slice comes first because dropping old data is the job; the other two weigh the price of each extra partition against its gain.

prompt: `enable_partitionwise_join` produced four per-month joins for `events_by_month` with itself, but one join for `events_by_month` with `events_by_day`. Why?
hint: What has to match between the two tables?

choices.text: The daily table has more rows
choices.why: Both hold the same five million rows.

choices.text: The setting only works on a table joined with itself
choices.why: It works for any two tables partitioned the same way.

choices.text: Months against days leave no pairs of matching bounds
choices.why: Right: partition-by-partition joins need the same key and the same bounds.

choices.text: events_by_day has no primary key
choices.why: The file added one, on (id, at).

prompt: Match each plan detail to what it shows.
hint: Four ways a plan shows partitions.

pairs.left: one partition under the `Append` for a literal date

right_distractors: a partition dropped from the table

prompt: A report filters `WHERE created_at::date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'` on a table partitioned by month on `created_at`, and reads all 36 partitions. What is the fix?
hint: Section 04.

choices.text: Add an index on `created_at::date`
choices.why: An index helps inside each partition; it does not let the planner skip any.

choices.text: Partition by day instead
choices.why: The condition would still be a function of the key, and the plan would have more partitions.

choices.text: Turn on enable_partitionwise_aggregate
choices.why: That changes how the partitions read are aggregated, not which are read.

choices.text: A range on `created_at` itself
choices.why: Right: `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-02-01'` prunes to one month.

prompt: An application's query is pruned to one month when typed in `psql` with a literal date. Through the application's driver, which prepares statements, what do you expect to see in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) EXECUTE`?
hint: After five executions.

choices.text: Every partition scanned, since prepared statements cannot prune
choices.why: They prune at run time; the lesson's EXECUTE read one month.

choices.text: A generic plan with `Subplans Removed`
choices.why: Right: the same month read, pruned when execution starts.

choices.text: An error about the missing date
choices.why: The date arrives with EXECUTE; nothing is missing.

choices.text: Exactly the psql plan, with the date written in
choices.why: A generic plan shows $1, not the date.
